title: Building Blocks in Economics: The Problem of Choice

learn.hook: The school canteen has 50 hot samosas at break time and 120 hungry students in the queue. Who gets one? Welcome to economics!
points: Human wants are unlimited: as soon as one want is satisfied, new wants appear.
Resources such as land, water, workers, machines, money and time are limited, and most of them can be put to more than one use.
Scarcity means that resources are limited compared with our wants. Because of scarcity, every person, family, business and country has to make choices.
Economic goods are scarce and usually carry a price, like rice, petrol or a notebook. Free goods, like the air we breathe, are available in plenty and cost nothing.
Goods and services are made using four factors of production: land, labour, capital and entrepreneurship. Their rewards are rent, wages, interest and profit.

example.q: Think it through: A very rich businesswoman in Mumbai can buy almost anything she likes. Does she face scarcity too?
steps: Scarcity is not the same as being poor. It means resources are limited compared with wants.
She still has only 24 hours in a day, so she must choose between a meeting, time with family and rest.
Her money is large but still limited compared with all the things she could want, so she must choose between projects too.
So scarcity touches everyone, rich or poor, and everyone has to make choices.
example.answer: Yes. Her time and even her money are limited compared with her wants, so she must also choose.

learn.reallife: Limited train seats during Diwali, water tankers shared by a colony in summer, and your own 24 hours split between study, play and sleep are all examples of scarcity.

games.title: Free good or economic good?
items: The air we breathe
Sunlight that dries clothes on the terrace
The wind that cools you on a beach
Bottled drinking water
Petrol for a scooter
A school notebook
A haircut at a salon
Electricity supplied to a home

games.title: Factors of production and their rewards

quiz.q: What is the basic economic problem that every society faces?
options: Wants are unlimited but resources are limited
Resources are unlimited but wants are limited
There is too much money in the economy
People do not want anything new
quiz.explain: Economics begins with scarcity: our wants keep growing, but the resources to satisfy them are limited, so we must choose.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the idea and thinks resources, not wants, are unlimited

quiz.q: Which of these is a free good?
quiz.explain: The air we breathe is available in plenty and nobody has to pay for it, so it is a free good. The others are scarce and have a price.
quiz.mistake: Thinks anything useful must be an economic good

quiz.q: In economics, what does 'scarcity' mean?
options: A good is not available anywhere at all
Resources are limited compared with people's wants
Only poor people cannot buy things
quiz.explain: Scarcity is about limited resources compared with wants. Even goods sold in every shop are scarce in this sense, because they cannot be made in endless amounts.
quiz.mistake: Confuses economic scarcity with a good being completely unavailable

quiz.q: A farmer in Punjab uses a tractor to plough his field. Which factor of production is the tractor?
quiz.explain: Capital means man-made goods, such as machines, tools and buildings, that are used to produce other goods. A tractor is capital.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the tractor is land because it is used on land

quiz.q: What is the reward earned by labour?
quiz.explain: Workers earn wages (or salaries) for their physical and mental work. Rent goes to land, interest to capital and profit to the entrepreneur.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the rewards of the four factors of production

quiz.q: A village has one empty plot of land. It could become a playground, a vegetable market or a health centre. What does this show?
quiz.explain: The same resource can be used in different ways, but only one use can be chosen at a time. This is why choices are needed.
quiz.mistake: Misses the idea that one resource can serve several purposes

quiz.q: Which statement about human wants is correct?
options: Wants stop once a person earns a salary
Wants are the same for everyone
When one want is satisfied, new wants usually arise
Wants and needs mean exactly the same thing
quiz.explain: Once Meera gets a bicycle, she may want a helmet, then a better bicycle. Wants keep coming back and growing, which is why they are called unlimited.
quiz.mistake: Believes that wants can be fully and finally satisfied

quiz.q: Why does even a very rich person have to make choices?
options: Shops do not sell to rich people
Time and other resources are still limited compared with wants
quiz.explain: Everyone has only 24 hours in a day, and even large resources are limited compared with wants. So scarcity, and the need to choose, affects everyone.
quiz.mistake: Thinks scarcity only affects people who are poor

teach.ask: Gappu flaps his wings: "Why can't everyone just have everything they want? Why do we have to choose at all?"
teach.praise: Tweet! Our wants never end, but resources are limited. That is scarcity, so we must choose. Now I see why I cannot eat ten samosas!
teach.nudge: Hmm, but are there enough resources for all the wants? What does that force us to do?

topics.title: Opportunity cost: the price of a choice

learn.hook: You choose to watch a cricket final instead of going to your friend's birthday party. The match was free. Or was it?
points: Every choice has a cost, because choosing one option means giving up others.
Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative that is given up when a choice is made. Only the next best option counts, not all the options together.
Opportunity cost is not always money. It can be time, fun, rest or a chance to learn something.
Good decisions compare the benefit of an option with its opportunity cost.

A production possibility curve shows the combinations of two goods an economy can make with its resources and technology. To make more of one good, it must make less of the other, and the amount given up is the opportunity cost.

example.q: Think it through: Arjun has a free Sunday evening. In order of his liking, he could study for Monday's test, play cricket with friends or watch a film. He chooses to study. What is his opportunity cost?
steps: List the options he did not choose: cricket and the film.
Find the next best of these. Cricket was his second choice.
Opportunity cost counts only the next best alternative, so the film is not added.
So the cost of studying is the cricket game he gave up.
example.answer: The game of cricket with his friends, his next best alternative.

learn.reallife: When your family spends savings on a new fridge instead of a holiday, or when a city uses land for a metro depot instead of a park, the option given up is the opportunity cost.

items.text: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best ___ given up.
Making a choice always means ___ something else.
Opportunity cost exists because resources are ___.
On a production possibility curve, making more of one good means making ___ of the other.

games.title: True or false?
items: Opportunity cost is only the next best alternative, not every option given up.
We count only the single best option that was given up, not all of them.
A free movie ticket has no opportunity cost.
You still give up the next best use of the time spent watching the movie.
Opportunity cost can be time, not just money.
Time spent on one activity cannot be spent on another, so it is a real cost.
Scarcity is the reason opportunity cost exists.
If resources were unlimited, we would never have to give anything up.
A government that spends money on a new highway gives up nothing.
The same money could have been used for something else, such as hospitals or schools.
When making a choice, comparing benefits with opportunity cost helps you decide better.
This is the basic idea of a careful economic decision.

quiz.q: What is opportunity cost?
options: The price printed on a product
The total of all options given up
The value of the next best alternative given up
The profit earned from a choice
quiz.explain: Opportunity cost is what you sacrifice by choosing: the value of the next best option you could have had instead.
quiz.mistake: Adds up all the options given up instead of only the next best one

quiz.q: Kavya can go to dance class, attend her cousin's birthday party or play badminton. She likes them in that order and goes to dance class. What is her opportunity cost?
options: The birthday party and badminton together
quiz.explain: Her next best option was the birthday party, so that is what she gave up. Badminton was only her third choice.
quiz.mistake: Counts every option not chosen instead of only the next best

quiz.q: A farmer's field can grow wheat worth ₹60,000, sugarcane worth ₹80,000 or vegetables worth ₹50,000 in a season. He grows sugarcane. What is his opportunity cost?
quiz.explain: Wheat at ₹60,000 is the best of the crops he did not grow, so it is the opportunity cost. We do not add the vegetables too.
quiz.mistake: Adds all the forgone options or picks the value of the chosen crop
steps: Options not chosen: wheat ₹60,000 and vegetables ₹50,000

items: Sugarcane (₹000)
Wheat (₹000)
Vegetables (₹000)

quiz.q: Sana spends two hours playing a mobile game instead of revising for her science test, which was her next best choice. What is the opportunity cost of the game?
options: The cost of the mobile phone
Nothing, because the game was free
The two hours of revision she gave up
quiz.explain: Opportunity cost is not always money. Here it is the revision time, and the learning, that she gave up.
quiz.mistake: Thinks opportunity cost must always be paid in rupees

quiz.q: A factory can make 6 cycles and 20 fans, or 4 cycles and 30 fans. If it moves from the first combination to the second, how many cycles is the opportunity cost of the extra 10 fans?
quiz.explain: To make 10 more fans, the factory gives up 6 − 4 = 2 cycles. Those 2 cycles are the opportunity cost.
quiz.mistake: Gives the number of cycles still made, or the fans gained, instead of the cycles given up

quiz.q: Rahul gets a free ticket to a three-hour film. Is watching the film really free for him?
options: Yes, because films have no cost
No, because the cinema loses money
No, because he gives up the next best use of those three hours
quiz.explain: Even without paying money, he uses three hours that could have gone to something else he valued. That is the opportunity cost.
quiz.mistake: Believes something with no money price has no cost at all

quiz.q: A city council uses a plot of land to build a parking lot instead of a park, which was the next best option. What is the opportunity cost of the parking lot?
options: The park that could have been built
The cars that will park there
The money paid for the parking lot
The road leading to the plot
quiz.explain: The park is the next best use of the land that was given up, so it is the opportunity cost.
quiz.mistake: Looks at what is gained or paid instead of what is given up

quiz.q: Why does opportunity cost exist?
options: Because scarce resources force us to choose between options
quiz.explain: If resources were unlimited, we could have everything. Scarcity forces choices, and every choice means giving something up.
quiz.mistake: Does not link opportunity cost to scarcity

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: "I picked mango ice cream instead of kulfi, which I like nearly as much. The ice cream cost money, but what else did it cost me?"
teach.praise: Chirp! The real cost of my mango ice cream is the kulfi I gave up, my next best choice. That is opportunity cost!
teach.nudge: But what did I miss out on when I chose the ice cream? Which other option was I giving up?

learn.hook: Should India grow more rice or more cotton? Use more machines or more workers? And who gets what is made? Every country must answer these questions.
points: Because of scarcity, every economy, from a family to a whole country, faces three central problems.
What to produce and how much: which goods and services to make with limited resources, for example more food grains or more cars, more schools or more roads.
How to produce: which technique to use. A labour-intensive technique uses more workers, while a capital-intensive technique uses more machines.
For whom to produce: how the goods and services, and the incomes earned, are shared among people.

In a market economy, buyers and sellers solve these problems through prices. In a centrally planned (command) economy, the government decides. A mixed economy, like India, uses both markets and government.

example.q: Think it through: A women's self-help group in an Odisha village has ₹50,000 and 10 members. Which central problems must it solve?
steps: What to produce: should they make pickles, papads or both, and how many packets?
How to produce: should they make them by hand (more labour) or buy a machine (more capital)?
For whom to produce: who will buy the products, and how will the earnings be shared among the 10 members?
These are the same three questions a whole country faces, only on a smaller scale.
example.answer: What to produce, how to produce and for whom to produce.

learn.reallife: When your family decides what to cook, whether to grind spices at home or buy them ready-made, and how to share the food, it is solving its own small 'central problems'.

games.title: Which central problem is it?
items: Should the country make more tractors or more buses?
Should a farmer grow cotton or soybean this season?
Should a bakery bake more bread or more cakes?
Should cloth be woven on handlooms or power looms?
Should a road be built with many workers or with big machines?
Should a factory use robots or hire more workers?
How should the profit of a cooperative be shared among its members?
Who should get the limited seats in a government hospital ward?
How should the national income be divided among different groups of people?

quiz.q: A textile factory is deciding whether to use more machines or hire more workers. Which central problem is this?
quiz.explain: Choosing between more machines and more workers is a choice of technique, which is the problem of how to produce.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the choice of technique with the choice of goods

quiz.q: A country must choose between producing more wheat or more cotton. Which central problem is this?
quiz.explain: Deciding which goods to make, and how much of each, is the problem of what to produce.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the choice of goods with the method of making them

quiz.q: The problem of 'for whom to produce' is about:
options: How the output and incomes are shared among people
quiz.explain: 'For whom' deals with distribution: who gets the goods and services and how income is divided in society.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'for whom' is about choosing the product or the method

quiz.q: Why do the central problems of an economy arise?
options: Because resources are limited and have alternative uses
Because there are too many shops
Because people do not like to work
Because money is printed by the government
quiz.explain: If resources were unlimited, no choices would be needed. Scarcity of resources with alternative uses creates the central problems.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the central problems to scarcity

quiz.q: A labour-intensive technique of production uses:
quiz.explain: Labour-intensive means relying more on human workers, like making handloom sarees, rather than heavy machinery.
quiz.mistake: Confuses labour-intensive with capital-intensive

quiz.q: In a market economy, how are the central problems mainly solved?
options: By buyers and sellers through the price mechanism
quiz.explain: In a market economy, prices set by demand and supply guide what is produced, how and for whom.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the government makes all decisions in every type of economy

quiz.q: What kind of economy does India have?
quiz.explain: India has a mixed economy: private businesses and markets work alongside the government, which runs some services such as railways and plans for public needs.
quiz.mistake: Thinks an economy must be either fully market or fully government-run

quiz.q: In a centrally planned (command) economy, who mainly decides what, how and for whom to produce?
quiz.explain: In a centrally planned economy, a government authority plans and decides how resources are used.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the command economy with the market economy

teach.ask: Gappu scratches his head: "Our bird kingdom has limited seeds and twigs. What big questions must we answer before we make anything?"
teach.praise: Tweet tweet! What to make, how to make it, and for whom. Three questions, all because of scarcity. I will call a bird meeting right now!
teach.nudge: You told me one or two questions. But isn't there another question about who will get the things we make, or how to make them?
